details.label: Discussion
details.text: Over the last hour, regional radar imagery showed scattered storms had developed and intensified along a stationary frontal zone from northern KS/MO into southern IA and western IL. Forcing for ascent has steadily increased this evening as a 30-40 kt low-level jet is developing and focusing low-level warm advection along the front. Lingering warm surface temperatures and dewpoints in the mid 70s F south of the front are supporting moderate to large buoyancy (2000-3000 J/kg of MUCAPE) despite modest mid-level lapse rate profiles. With continued forcing along the frontal axis, storm coverage is expected to increase through the overnight hours. Area VADs show low-level shear has increased along with the aforementioned low-level jet. Much of this shear is concentrated in the lowest 3km, with deep-layer shear comparatively limited due to weak flow aloft around 20 kt. This could support some supercell structures, though the weaker deep-layer shear casts some uncertainty on the longevity of storm organization. Still, the large buoyancy could support some risk for hail. Additionally, any clustering could allow for strong to severe gusts. However, this should become less likely with time as the boundary layer stabilizes overnight. CAM guidance shows storms increasing in coverage and gradually shifting eastward along the front through the night. Some runs do show more clustering which could support a greater localized risk, though this is uncertain as the trend should be for storms to become elevated. Thus, while some severe risk is possible over the next few hours, the lack of a more focused and organized severe risk suggests a WW is currently unlikely
